stem: A magnetic pole of bar magnet with pole strength of 100 A m is 20 cm away from the centre of a bar magnet. Bar magnet has pole strength of 200 A m  and has a length 5 cm. If the magnetic pole is on the axis of the bar magnet, find the force on the magnetic pole.
context:
Solve the following Problems.

[Take \(\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) SI units, i.e. \(\mu_{0}/4\pi = 10^{-7}\) — the value stated by this chapter's own worked Examples 12.1 and 12.2. The exercise prints no constants line of its own.]
our_solution:
**Data.** Pole strength of the isolated pole \(q_{m} = 100\,\text{A m}\); distance from the centre of the bar magnet \(r = 20\,\text{cm} = 0.2\,\text{m}\); pole strength of the bar magnet \(q_{M} = 200\,\text{A m}\); its magnetic length \(2l = 5\,\text{cm} = 0.05\,\text{m}\); the pole lies on the axis of the bar magnet.

**Step 1 — magnetic moment of the bar magnet.**
\(M = q_{M}\times 2l = 200 \times 0.05 = 10\,\text{A m}^{2}\)

**Step 2 — field of the bar magnet at the location of the pole.** The point is on the axis and \(r \gg 2l\), so the short-dipole axial field of Eq. (12.3) applies:
\(B_{a} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{2M}{r^{3}} = \dfrac{10^{-7}\times 2 \times 10}{(0.2)^{3}} = \dfrac{2\times 10^{-6}}{8\times 10^{-3}}\)
\(B_{a} = 2.5\times 10^{-4}\,\text{T}\)

**Step 3 — force on the pole.** From the magnetic entry of Table 12.1, \(\vec{F} = q_{m}\vec{B}\):
\(F = q_{m}B_{a} = 100 \times 2.5\times 10^{-4}\)

\(F = 2.5\times 10^{-2}\,\text{N}\)

The force acts along the axis of the bar magnet, and is one of attraction or repulsion according to which pole of the bar magnet faces the given pole. This agrees with the answer printed in the book.

[Note: the short-dipole formula is an approximation here, since \(2l\) is not utterly negligible against \(r\). Using the exact two-pole expression \(F = q_{m}\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}q_{M}\left[\dfrac{1}{(r-l)^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{(r+l)^{2}}\right]\) gives \(2.58\times 10^{-2}\,\text{N}\), about 3% higher. The printed answer is the short-dipole value.]

stem: A magnet makes an angle of \(45^{\circ}\) with the horizontal in a plane making an angle of \(30^{\circ}\) with the magnetic meridian.  Find the true value of the dip angle at the place.
context:
Solve the following Problems.

[Take \(\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) SI units, i.e. \(\mu_{0}/4\pi = 10^{-7}\) — the value stated by this chapter's own worked Examples 12.1 and 12.2. The exercise prints no constants line of its own.]
our_solution:
**Idea.** A dip needle reads the true dip only when it swings in the magnetic meridian. Turned into any other vertical plane it reads an **apparent** dip, because the plane picks up only the component of the horizontal field that lies in it, while the vertical field is unchanged.

**Set-up.** Let \(\phi\) be the true dip and let the plane of swing make an angle \(\theta\) with the magnetic meridian. The vertical component in that plane is still \(B_{V}\); the horizontal component resolved into the plane is \(B_{H}\cos\theta\). Hence the apparent dip \(\phi'\) obeys
\(\tan\phi' = \dfrac{B_{V}}{B_{H}\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\tan\phi}{\cos\theta}\)
using Eq. (12.10), \(\tan\phi = B_{V}/B_{H}\). Rearranging,
\(\tan\phi = \tan\phi' \cos\theta\)

**Substituting.** Here the magnet settles at \(\phi' = 45^{\circ}\) in a plane at \(\theta = 30^{\circ}\) to the magnetic meridian:
\(\tan\phi = \tan 45^{\circ} \times \cos 30^{\circ} = 1 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 0.866\)

\(\therefore \phi = \tan^{-1}(0.866) \approx 40^{\circ}54'\)

The true dip is smaller than the apparent dip, as it must be, since \(\cos\theta < 1\) for any plane away from the magnetic meridian. This agrees with the answer printed in the book.

stem: Two small and similar bar magnets have magnetic dipole moment of 1.0 A m\(^{2}\) each. They are kept in a plane in such a way that their axes are perpendicular to each other. A line drawn through the axis of one magnet passes through the center of other magnet. If the distance between their centers is 2 m, find the magnitude of magnetic field at the mid point of the line joining their centers.
context:
Solve the following Problems.

[Take \(\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) SI units, i.e. \(\mu_{0}/4\pi = 10^{-7}\) — the value stated by this chapter's own worked Examples 12.1 and 12.2. The exercise prints no constants line of its own.]
our_solution:
**Geometry.** Call the magnets 1 and 2, each of moment \(m = 1.0\,\text{A m}^{2}\), with centres \(2\,\text{m}\) apart, so the mid-point O of the line joining the centres is \(r = 1\,\text{m}\) from each. The axes are perpendicular to each other, and the line joining the centres is drawn along the axis of one magnet. Therefore, taking magnet 1 to be the one whose axis lies along that line:

- O lies on the **axis** of magnet 1;
- O lies on the **equator** of magnet 2, because magnet 2's axis is perpendicular to the joining line.

**Field due to magnet 1 (axial).** By Eq. (12.3),
\(B_{1} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^{3}} = \dfrac{10^{-7}\times 2 \times 1.0}{1^{3}} = 2\times 10^{-7}\,\text{T}\)
directed along \(\vec{m}_{1}\), i.e. along the joining line.

**Field due to magnet 2 (equatorial).** By Eq. (12.4),
\(B_{2} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{r^{3}} = \dfrac{10^{-7}\times 1.0}{1^{3}} = 1\times 10^{-7}\,\text{T}\)
directed opposite to \(\vec{m}_{2}\), i.e. perpendicular to the joining line.

**Resultant.** The two contributions are mutually perpendicular, so they add in quadrature:
\(B = \sqrt{B_{1}^{2} + B_{2}^{2}} = \sqrt{(2\times 10^{-7})^{2} + (1\times 10^{-7})^{2}}\)
\(B = 10^{-7}\sqrt{4 + 1}\)

\(B = \sqrt{5}\times 10^{-7}\,\text{T} \approx 2.24\times 10^{-7}\,\text{T}\)

Its direction makes an angle \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{B_{2}}{B_{1}}\right) = \tan^{-1}(0.5) \approx 26^{\circ}34'\) with the joining line. This agrees with the answer printed in the book.
